issues.legal_issue: The prosecution evidence was sufficient to sustain the convictions despite the defence claim that the deceased was killed during a dacoity.
material_facts: Several witnesses identified the appellants and described their participation in taking the deceased into the residential part of the premises, where he was shot.
The deceased's mother testified that she saw one appellant shoot him.
The informant promptly reported the incident, and the evidence showed prior hostility between the appellants and the deceased and his family.
The medical evidence established that the deceased died a violent death.
The defence produced no evidence supporting its claim that a dacoity had occurred.
issues.conclusion: The eyewitnesses were credible, the defence theory was unsupported, and there was no reason to interfere with the convictions.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the prosecution evidence as a whole, including the credibility of the witnesses and the consistency of their accounts with the medical evidence and surrounding circumstances. It relied on no earlier case for this issue.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_conviction and credible_eyewitness_accounts and (prompt_report or evidence_of_prior_hostility) and unsupported_alternative_account

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: A convicted person challenged a criminal conviction in an appeal.
predicates.credible_eyewitness_accounts: Several witnesses gave credible accounts identifying the accused and describing their involvement in the fatal incident.
predicates.prompt_report: The informant reported the incident soon after it occurred.
predicates.evidence_of_prior_hostility: The evidence showed prior hostility between the accused and the victim or the victim's family.
predicates.unsupported_alternative_account: The defence proposed a different account of the death but presented no evidence supporting it.

issues.definition: When a criminal appeal challenges a conviction, credible eyewitness accounts together with a prompt report or evidence of prior hostility, and an unsupported alternative account, result in the conviction being upheld.

issues.legal_issue: The prosecution's failure to examine a child who first alerted a witness to the presence of intruders did not undermine the case supported by reliable witnesses.
material_facts: A child told the deceased's mother that intruders had entered the shop.
The prosecution did not examine the child.
Several other witnesses whose testimony the Court found reliable supported the prosecution case.
issues.conclusion: The failure to examine the child did not adversely affect the prosecution case.
issues.legal_principle: In the circumstances, the omission was not material because a large number of reliable witnesses supported the prosecution case. The Court relied on no earlier case for this issue.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: A convicted person challenged a criminal conviction in an appeal.
predicates.a_witness_was_not_examined: The prosecution did not call a person who had information about the incident.
predicates.multiple_reliable_witnesses_supported_th: Several witnesses whose testimony was found reliable supported the prosecution account.

issues.definition: When a witness is not examined in a criminal appeal against conviction, the omission is not fatal if multiple reliable witnesses support the prosecution case.

issues.legal_issue: A participant who did not personally assault the victim could be convicted for murder where his conduct furthered the group's common intention to kill.
material_facts: The accused arrived together with others, carrying firearms.
Some members of the group took the victim into the residence, where one of them shot him.
The accused prevented witnesses from intervening while the victim was taken and attacked.
The group left together after the shooting.
issues.conclusion: The accused shared the group's common intention to commit murder and was rightly convicted even though he did not personally assault the victim.
issues.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code provides for joint liability where persons commit a criminal act in furtherance of their common intention. Common intention may be formed before or during the occurrence, but must precede the act constituting the offence; it may be inferred from the circumstances. Each participant need not personally assault the victim if each plays a role furthering the common intention. The Court applied Suresh v. State of U.P., (2001) 3 SCC 673, and distinguished Parshuram Singh v. State of Bihar, JT 2002 (1) SC 407, as turning on its particular facts.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_conviction and armed_group_arrived_together and accused_obstructed_rescue and other_group_members_killed_victim and group_actions_supported_shared_intent

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: A convicted person challenged a criminal conviction in an appeal.
predicates.armed_group_arrived_together: The accused arrived together with other participants, carrying weapons.
predicates.accused_obstructed_rescue: The accused prevented other people from intervening or rescuing the victim.
predicates.other_group_members_killed_victim: Other members of the group took the victim and one of them inflicted the fatal injury.
predicates.group_actions_supported_shared_intent: The participants' coordinated conduct before, during, and after the attack supported the inference that they shared an intention to kill the victim.

issues.definition: When an armed group arrives together, an accused obstructs rescue, other group members kill the victim, and the group's coordinated actions support a shared intention, joint liability for murder is upheld in a criminal appeal against conviction.
